what: A mechanical multiplier by tan θ. Motor A turns a straight radial guide about a fixed pivot (1:1), setting the angle θ. Motor B turns the spindle of a small linear actuator that sets the reach x of a carriage; one spindle turn is only about 1.2 mm, so 2,388° of motor B moves it 8 mm. A captured pivot slides in a sleeve on the angled guide and in a transverse slider at reach x. That slider’s position y has no motor: it is simply where the two guides cross. The program visits eight (θ, x) pairs: (0°, 40 mm), (15°, 32), (15°, 48), (−15°, 48), (−15°, 32), (atan ¼ ≈ 14.04°, 32), (atan ⅙ ≈ 9.46°, 48) and (0°, 40).
try: Reset, then Run. Stages 1–2: at +15° the reach goes from 32 to 48 mm. Predict y first: 8.57 mm, then 12.86 mm, so 16 mm of reach gives 4.29 mm of output (gain tan 15° ≈ 0.268).
Stages 3–4 use the same reaches at −15°. The output goes negative: the slope of the guide sets the sign of the gain.
Stages 5–6 end at (32 mm, 14.04°) and (48 mm, 9.46°). Both give y = 8 mm. Watch y during the move between them: does it stay at 8 mm?
Stage 7 returns to (40 mm, 0°). At zero angle y = 0 whatever the reach.
why: Every point on a straight line through the origin at angle θ satisfies y/x = tan θ. The transverse slider holds the pivot at reach x and the sleeve keeps it on the angled line, so y = x·tan θ. At a fixed angle the output is proportional to the reach: the angle sets the gain, including its sign. Because the sleeve slides, there is no fixed link length to bend the relationship, as a connecting rod would. The relation is exact geometry, not an approximation, but tan θ grows quickly towards 90°, so a small angle error at a large angle gives a large output error. The ±15° range keeps the gain between −0.268 and +0.268.
matters: Analogue computers and naval fire-control equipment multiplied in this way: a slotted guide turned to an angle scales a linear input. A pantograph copies motion at a fixed scale; here the scale itself is an input, which makes this a variable-gain stage. Product Plotter uses the same crossing-guides idea to multiply two lengths.
question: Stages 5 and 6 both end at y = 8 mm. Does y stay at 8 mm while both motors move between them?
answer: No. The endpoints match because 32 × ¼ = 8 and 48 × ⅙ = 8. Between them the program changes angle and reach in step with time, not along the curve x·tan θ = 8. Halfway, at x ≈ 40 mm and θ ≈ 11.75°, y ≈ 40 × tan 11.75° ≈ 8.32 mm, so the output rises slightly above 8 mm and comes back.
further: Why are the motor speeds so different? Motor B needs about 299° per millimetre of reach, while motor A turns the guide directly. The program scales each speed so that both inputs finish a stage together.

Construction limits reported by the supplier: in the source meshes one actuator mounting pin intersects the actuator’s lug, and the simulator’s screw primitive does not model thread contact. A real build would need a fitting check.

In a headless Robot Lab simulation of the shipped program, the slider matched x·tan θ within 0.001 mm at every frame, using the guide angle measured from its pose. The guide itself stopped up to 0.17° past its motor targets (inside the program’s 0.5° arrival tolerance), so the two equal-output endpoints came out at 8.09 and 8.15 mm and the transit peaked at about 8.41 mm. That is a simulation observation, not a physical test.
formula: y = x·tan θ; sleeve position along the guide s = x / cos θ; at fixed θ, Δy = tan θ·Δx. (15°, 32 mm) → 8.574 mm; (15°, 48 mm) → 12.862 mm; full span ±12.862 mm. θ = motor A angle (1:1). x = 40 mm − 0.00335 mm per degree × motor B angle (1.206 mm per spindle turn). Software envelopes: θ within ±16°, x within 31.2–48.8 mm.
